Author `CONTRIBUTING.md` at the repo root. Documents: project licensing (dual MIT/Apache-2.0), DCO/CLA stance (DCO sign-off required, no CLA), contributor workflow (fork-and-PR), local validation expected before opening a PR, the Argo-CI-on-fork caveat (because iad-ci is private and external forks cannot trigger CI on their branch), and links to other policy docs (CODE_OF_CONDUCT, SECURITY).

## Why this matters

CONTRIBUTING.md is the first place a new contributor reads. It MUST be clear that CI runs on a private cluster and contributors cannot self-serve test runs; the maintainer-trigger model is unusual enough that surprise on first PR is guaranteed without explicit documentation. The local-validation checklist also reduces the maintainer's review burden — well-prepared PRs land faster.

## Implementation guidance

- File location: `/CONTRIBUTING.md` at repo root
- Sections (in order):
  1. **Project licensing** — dual MIT OR Apache-2.0, no CLA, DCO sign-off required (use `git commit --signoff`)
  2. **Code of conduct** — link to CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
  3. **Reporting security issues** — link to SECURITY.md (DO NOT open public issues for vulns)
  4. **Development setup**:
     - Clone, install Rust 1.78+, `cargo build --workspace --locked`
     - Install OCR dependencies if developing OCR features (Tesseract instructions per platform)
     - Run tests: `cargo test --workspace --features default`
  5. **Local validation expected before opening a PR**:
     - `cargo test --features default` (all green)
     - `cargo clippy --all-targets --features default -- -D warnings`
     - `cargo bloat --release --features default` (binary size within budget; target <= 4 MB stripped)
     - `cargo audit` (no medium+ advisories)
     - `cargo deny check licenses` (no rejected licenses)
     - `cargo fmt --check`
  6. **CI on forks (the Argo-CI caveat)**:
     - "Because CI runs on the private iad-ci cluster, external contributors cannot trigger CI from their fork."
     - "A maintainer will trigger the pdftract-ci Argo workflow against your branch (results posted as a PR comment)."
     - Expected response time: 48 hours
  7. **PR template requirements** — link to .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md
  8. **Commit message style** — Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `perf:`, `docs:`, `chore:`, `BREAKING CHANGE`)
  9. **Issue triage** — link to .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/
- Style: Markdown; ~300-500 lines; concrete commands over prose

## Critical considerations

- The DCO-only stance (no CLA) is a deliberate choice — CLAs deter casual contributors; DCO is sufficient for permissive-license projects
- The Argo-CI caveat is unusual; emphasise it to avoid contributor frustration
- The local-validation checklist MUST match the per-step requirements in `pdftract-ci` so a green local run predicts a green CI run
- Conventional Commits are required because release notes are auto-generated from commit history (git-cliff)
- The 48-hour maintainer-trigger window is a commitment — meeting it requires monitoring `gh pr list --label needs-ci` regularly; consider a Slack/Discord notification bot for first-time PRs (deferred to v1.1+)

- All nine sections above are present

issue.description:
## Scope

Implement header-row detection for tables. A row is a header row if (a) all cells contain only bold-flagged glyphs, OR (b) the StructTree marks the row's StructElem as TH (table header). Tag header rows in the output (Cell.is_header_row = true; Table.header_rows = count).

## Why this matters

Header tags drive Markdown table rendering, HTML thead, and downstream tools that recognise the header for CSV export. Without explicit header marking, every renderer falls back to "first row is header" heuristic - wrong on tables with multi-row headers (financial reports), tables with footer totals (invoices), and tables with no header (matrices).

## Implementation guidance

- Bold detection (per cell): inspect each span's font flags
  - PDF font /Flags bit 19 (ForceBold) = bold
  - OR PostScript name contains "Bold" / "Bd" / "Black" / "Heavy"
  - OR /FontWeight stylistic attribute >= 700 (rare; OpenType only)
- Cell is bold if 100% of its non-whitespace glyphs are in bold fonts
- Row is bold-header if 100% of its cells are bold (single-cell rows do not qualify; the row must have at least 2 cells with content)
- StructTree TH detection: if 7.1 produced a structure tree, find the StructElem covering this cell's bbox by MCID lookup; row is TH-header if every cell in the row maps to a TH StructElem (TR > TH chain)
- Multi-row headers: contiguous header rows from the top of the table all become headers (Table.header_rows >= 1)
- If both signals are present, both confirm; if conflict (bold body row, no TH tag), bold wins per body data design

## Critical considerations

- Font weight detection from PostScript name is heuristic; ForceBold flag is authoritative when present
- StructTree TH is only available on tagged PDFs (7.1) - graceful fallback to bold-only detection otherwise
- "All bold" includes punctuation and digits; whitespace-only cells skipped from the bold check
- Empty rows (all cells empty) are NOT headers even if technically all spans satisfy the test (zero spans pass vacuously)
- Footer rows ("Total", "Grand Total") may also be bold - this task does NOT detect footers; only headers from the top of the table

## Acceptance criteria

- Critical test (from plan): merged header cell spanning 3 columns - header row detected (colspan handled in 7.2.5)
- Unit tests: bold header row, plain header row + TH tag, no header at all, multi-row header (2 contiguous)
- Output: Cell.is_header_row: bool, Table.header_rows: u32
- Documented heuristic in docs/research/table-structure-reconstruction.md

## References

- Plan section: 7.2 line 2574 (header detection)
- 7.1 StructTree TH (alternate signal)
- 7.2.3 cell content (provides spans + font info)
- docs/research/table-structure-reconstruction.md

issue.description:
## Scope

Build the per-search matcher from GrepArgs. Compile PATTERN into either a literal Aho-Corasick automaton (-F mode, default) or a regex::Regex (-E mode). Apply -i (case-insensitive) and -w (word-boundary) wrappers. Provide a uniform Matcher::find_iter(text) -> Iter<MatchRange> API used by the per-span matcher.

## Why this matters

Literal-by-default is critical for performance on common queries (most users grep for words, not regex). Aho-Corasick handles single-pattern literal matching with bytewise SIMD on most platforms; regex::Regex provides the full ECMAScript-ish syntax for power users. Wrappers for -i and -w keep the matcher creation in one place and the per-span loop uniform.

## Implementation guidance

- Crates: regex = "1.10", aho-corasick = "1" (transitive dep of regex; bring in directly for literal mode)
- Matcher enum: Literal(AhoCorasick) | Regex(Regex)
- Build:
  - Default (-F): aho_corasick::AhoCorasick::builder().ascii_case_insensitive(args.ignore_case).build([&args.pattern])
  - -E: regex::RegexBuilder::new(&args.pattern).case_insensitive(args.ignore_case).build()?
  - Both modes: if -w, wrap pattern with word-boundary: regex mode prepends \b and appends \b; literal mode adds a post-match check (preceding char and following char are non-word)
- MatchRange { start: usize, end: usize } - byte offsets into the span text
- API: matcher.find_iter(text: &str) -> Box<dyn Iterator<Item = MatchRange> + '_>
- For -v (invert): invert at the SPAN granularity, not match granularity - a span has zero matches -> emit a synthetic "non-match" record covering the whole span text
- Pattern compile errors: return clap-friendly error message with line:col context
- Empty pattern: error "PATTERN may not be empty"

## Critical considerations

- aho-corasick (literal) is typically faster than regex for one needle; do not fall through to regex when -F is requested
- -i case folding is ASCII-only by default; full Unicode case folding optional (regex with unicode_case_insensitive feature) - default to ASCII to keep binary slim
- -w word-boundary: Unicode word characters via regex's \b implementation; for literal mode, use a simple ASCII-word post-check (suffices for most use cases)
- Multi-line PATTERN values (containing newlines) should be allowed - regex handles via (?s); literal handles via raw bytes
- Pattern containing null byte: reject with error

## Acceptance criteria

- Critical test: literal "INVOICE" matches in 100 PDFs - expected count returned
- Critical test: regex "\$\d+\.\d{2}" - all dollar-amount patterns found
- Unit tests: -i case folding, -w word boundary (no match for "fish" in "fisheries"), -v invert produces non-match spans
- Pattern compile error gives line:col message
- Empty pattern rejected at parse time

## References

- Plan section: 7.8 line 2716 (-E full regex), 2717 (-F literal default), 2715 (-i), 2718 (-w)
- Plan Critical tests (lines 2800-2801): literal + regex examples
- 7.8.1 (GrepArgs source)
- 7.8.4 (per-span matcher consumer)

All acceptance criteria PASS. Commits: 66b3eff, 3d4f29b. Verification note: notes/pdftract-jmh6w.md
issue.description:
## Scope

Bridge tokio's async executor with rayon's synchronous work pool. Each POST handler uses tokio::task::spawn_blocking to run extraction on tokio's blocking thread pool (separate from the async reactor). Within the blocking task, rayon provides per-document page-level parallelism. Document this concurrency model in module rustdoc + serve --help text.

## Why this matters

The naive approach (run extraction in the async handler directly) blocks the tokio reactor, breaking concurrency. The naive alternative (per-request rayon::spawn) leaks rayon threads across requests, breaking thread-pool scheduling. The right architecture: tokio spawn_blocking for per-request isolation; rayon for per-document parallelism within that blocking task. Rayon's default pool sizing (logical CPU count) is reused.

## Implementation guidance

- Pattern in each handler:
  let result = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || {
      // Inside this closure, rayon parallelism is normal
      extract_inner(pdf_bytes, options)
  }).await.map_err(|e| handle_join_err(e))??;
- tokio's blocking pool default size = 512 threads (tokio default); plenty for typical concurrent serve workload
- Rayon's default pool size = num_cpus::get(); shared across all spawn_blocking tasks
- No explicit pool configuration unless user passes --threads N (advanced); document in serve --help
- Handle JoinError (e.g. spawn_blocking task panicked): convert to 500 with error code INTERNAL_PANIC
- For streaming endpoint: use spawn_blocking to drive rayon producer + Receiver feeds the async stream

## Critical considerations

- DO NOT call .block_on or wait synchronously on async from inside spawn_blocking (deadlock risk)
- Rayon's global pool is shared; if you call rayon::par_iter from inside spawn_blocking, the work goes to the global pool (correct behavior)
- tokio runtime default-flavor multi-thread is required (single-thread would serialize requests)
- Document in serve --help: "Concurrency: rayon for per-document page parallelism, tokio for per-request concurrency. Default pool sizes use num_cpus."
- Critical test (line 2146): 8 concurrent requests with 8 simultaneous PDFs all complete

## Acceptance criteria

- 8 concurrent requests via curl -P 8 -> all 8 complete in roughly same wallclock as 1 (proves parallelism, not serialization)
- /health responds in < 100 ms during 8 concurrent extractions (proves /health doesn't go through blocking pool)
- Rayon par_iter inside spawn_blocking works as expected (within-document parallelism)
- Module rustdoc + serve --help text documents the concurrency model

## References

- Plan section: Phase 6.4 concurrency (line 2132)
- tokio::task::spawn_blocking docs
issue.title: 6.4.3: rayon+tokio concurrency bridge (spawn_blocking pattern in all handlers)

issue.description:
## Scope

Build a compile-time table of the 14 Adobe Standard fonts with their AFM-derived per-glyph widths, FontBBox, ascent, descent, italic angle, and AGL-equivalent encoding (StandardEncoding or SymbolEncoding/ZapfDingbatsEncoding). When `classify_font` returns `Type1Std14`, all metric lookups MUST come from this registry — no font program is ever embedded for these.

## Why this matters

Standard 14 fonts are explicitly allowed to omit the font program (`/FontFile*`). Without a registry, every Std-14 lookup fails. Pdfminer.six and pypdf rely on bundled AFM files at runtime; pdftract compiles the metrics into the binary for zero-runtime-dependency operation.

## Implementation guidance

- Source AFM-derived widths from the public Adobe Core 14 AFM files (PDF-1.7 Annex D); commit the extracted JSON to `crates/pdftract-core/build/std14-metrics.json`.
- `build.rs` reads the JSON and emits a `phf::Map<&'static str, &'static Std14Metrics>` keyed by canonical name (post-prefix-strip).
- Struct: `pub struct Std14Metrics { widths: &'static [u16; 256], ascent: i16, descent: i16, italic_angle: f32, font_bbox: [i16; 4], encoding: NamedEncoding }`.
- Symbol and ZapfDingbats use `SymbolEncoding` / `ZapfDingbatsEncoding` (not StandardEncoding) — preserve that distinction.

## Critical considerations

- Std-14 widths are indexed by character CODE (not glyph id). Code 0x20 = space width.
- italic_angle is in degrees as a signed float; negative = oblique to the right.
- Some PDF producers embed a font program for a Std-14 font anyway — when present, prefer the embedded metrics for consistency but fall back to this registry on parse failure.

## Acceptance criteria

- Lookup of all 14 names returns valid metrics.
- Subset-prefixed name `ABCDEF+Helvetica` resolves to Helvetica via the strip helper.
- Width tables sum to known AFM values within 1 unit (rounding tolerance).
- Binary footprint < 60 KB for the registry (verify via `cargo bloat`).

## References

- Plan section: Phase 2.1, "Standard 14 font (no embedding)" critical test (line 1312)
- ISO 32000-1 Annex D

issue.description:
## Scope

Parse linearization hint stream (/H in Linearized dict) and use it for prefetch optimization when extracting from remote linearized PDFs.

Hint stream is flate-decoded stream of byte offsets and lengths per page (page offset hints). Allows pdftract to predict byte ranges per page and prefetch BEFORE Phase 1.4 dereferences each page on demand.

Format (PDF spec Annex F): bit-packed records describing each page's content stream byte range; plus shared-object section for objects referenced by multiple pages.

## Implementation guidance

- Public API:
  - parse_hint_stream(bytes: &[u8]) -> Option<HintTable>
  - HintTable::predict_page_range(page_index: u32) -> Option<Range<u64>>
  - HintTable::predict_shared_objects() -> Vec<Range<u64>>
- Bit-packed parsing: use manual BitReader over decoded bytes (no crate needed)
- Phase 1.3 linearization handler extracts /H offset+length, calls parse_hint_stream
- Prefetch integration: linearization handler calls source.prefetch(range.start, range.len()) for each predicted page in --pages range
- Prefetch is OPTIMISTIC: if prediction wrong, on-demand fetch still works; no correctness impact

## Critical considerations

- Hint stream format is trickiest part of PDF linearization to parse; refer to PDF spec Annex F.2
- Malformed hint stream emits STRUCT_INVALID_HINT_STREAM and disables prefetch; document still parses correctly (slower)
- Prefetch is PERFORMANCE optimization; extraction still works without
- Critical test: document with linearized hint stream — page-offset hints utilized to predict and prefetch
- Performance benefit: prefetch makes 5-page extraction ~30% faster (saves round-trip latency by pipelining)
- Cache interaction: prefetch populates HttpRangeSource's LRU cache; on-demand reads hit cache
- Hint stream is OPTIONAL even in linearized PDFs; if /H absent, this code never invoked
- For Phase 1, parser may be MINIMAL: just header + page-offset records; skip shared-object records. Covers ~90% of perf benefit
- Bit-packing: each field's width given in header; use generic `read_bits(reader, width: u8) -> u32` helper

## Acceptance criteria

- parse_hint_stream returns Some(HintTable) for valid hint stream
- parse_hint_stream returns None for malformed hint stream (STRUCT_INVALID_HINT_STREAM diagnostic)
- HintTable::predict_page_range returns correct byte range for page in known fixture (verify against qpdf --linearize-stats)
- Critical test: extracting pages 47-52 of 500-page linearized fixture with prefetch is >= 30% faster than without (mock server timeline)
- Prefetch OPTIONAL: extraction succeeds if hint stream absent or malformed
- proptest: random byte sequences fed to parse_hint_stream never panic
- INV-8 maintained

## References

- Plan section: Phase 1.8 line 1247 (hint stream for prefetch); critical test line 1277
- PDF spec Annex F.2
- Phase 1.3 (linearization handler — calls into this)
- INV-8
issue.title: Implement linearized PDF hint stream parser + prefetch optimization for remote sources

issue.description:
## Scope

Augment the YAML profile loader to reject any profile YAML containing top-level password, token, secret, or api_key keys (case-insensitive, also matches sub-keys at any depth). Emit a PROFILE_SECRETS_FORBIDDEN diagnostic and fail the load with a non-zero exit code (when invoked via pdftract profiles validate or install). The check runs both at install time and at load time so that a tampered profile cached on disk is also caught.

## Why this matters

Line 927 in the plan codifies this: "Profile loaders MUST reject any YAML containing top-level password:, token:, secret:, or api_key: keys with PROFILE_SECRETS_FORBIDDEN. Profiles are checked into git in the profiles/community/ directory; secrets in them would be a public disclosure incident." This is an A5 (operator misconfig) attack-class mitigation: an unwitting user shipping a profile with their API key into the public profile repo would expose that key to the world. The loader catches the mistake before publication.

## Implementation guidance

- File to modify: pdftract-core/src/profiles/loader.rs (or wherever serde_yaml::from_str is called for profile YAML)
- Step 1: parse YAML into a generic serde_yaml::Value first (before deserializing into the typed Profile struct)
- Step 2: walk the Value tree and check every key: case-fold and trim; if matches one of {password, passwd, token, secret, api_key, apikey, api-key, auth_token, auth-token, bearer, key, credential, credentials} AT THE TOP LEVEL or NESTED inside fields/extraction/metadata blocks -> reject
- Step 3: if rejected, return Err with a PROFILE_SECRETS_FORBIDDEN diagnostic carrying: file path, key path (e.g. fields.api_key), line number (serde_yaml::Value preserves position via the yaml-rust2 backend)
- Allowed: the substring api in field NAMES like "vendor_api" is fine; the check is on KEY names ONLY, not values or strings that contain those substrings
- Step 4: the same check runs at install time (pdftract profiles install my.yaml: reject if secrets present) AND at load time (extract --profile pre-installed.yaml: reject again -- defense in depth)
- Add to diagnostics catalogue: PROFILE_SECRETS_FORBIDDEN as a load error diagnostic

## Critical considerations

- The reject-list is case-insensitive (Password and PASSWORD both caught)
- The check is keys-only: a regex value like ".*password.*" is fine (a user may want to extract a password label from a document) -- the reject is on key names because keys define the YAML structure that ends up in source control
- A separator-tolerant comparison: api_key, apiKey, api-key, api.key all map to the same canonical lowercased form for the reject check
- The diagnostic MUST include the key path and approximate line number; without that the user cannot find what to delete
- Test fixture: a profile YAML that has fields: api_key: in it; load attempt fails with PROFILE_SECRETS_FORBIDDEN
- Built-in profiles are also subject to this check at compile time via a build.rs guard or a unit test that loads every built-in profile

## Acceptance criteria

- Profile loader rejects YAML with the reject-key-list at any depth

## Scope

Author the Tera template scaffolding for the 8 subprocess-based SDKs under `templates/sdk-skeleton/<lang>/`: `node/`, `go/`, `java/`, `dotnet/`, `ruby/`, `php/`, `swift/`, plus the `python-subprocess/` fallback path (the PyO3 native binding is hand-written and is not a generator target). The generator is useless without templates. Each language has distinct idioms (file layout, import conventions, error patterns, package metadata) that must be captured in the template; the templates ARE the per-language idiom specification. issue.close_reason: Implemented ASCIIHexDecode filter per PDF spec 7.4.2. Odd-length final pair handling (pad with low nibble=0), PDF spec whitespace (7.2.2), invalid byte handling (continue per INV-8), fixed bomb limit enforcement. All 11 acceptance criteria tests PASS. Commit 6aefd76. Verification note at notes/pdftract-lhq9t.md
issue.description:
## Scope

Hand-written ASCIIHexDecode filter per PDF spec 7.4.2. Decodes hex digit pairs (0-9, A-F, a-f) into binary bytes. Whitespace ignored between digits. > terminator ends the stream. Odd-length final pair pads with low nibble = 0.

## Why this matters

ASCIIHex is the simplest of the 9 stream-decoder filters; trivial to implement but commonly used to encode short binary tokens (Identity-H CMap data, small image data). Hex-paired encoding is human-readable in PDF source which is why some PDF generators (TeX/LaTeX, older Acrobat versions) use it.

## Implementation guidance

- State machine:
  ```
  let mut high_nibble: Option<u8> = None;
  for byte in input {
      if byte == b'>' { break }  // terminator
      if is_whitespace(byte) { continue }
      let n = match byte {
          b'0'..=b'9' => byte - b'0',
          b'a'..=b'f' => byte - b'a' + 10,
          b'A'..=b'F' => byte - b'A' + 10,
          _ => { emit STRUCT_INVALID_HEX; continue }
      };
      match high_nibble {
          None => high_nibble = Some(n),
          Some(hi) => { emit (hi << 4) | n; high_nibble = None }
      }
  }
  // Odd-length final: pad with 0
  if let Some(hi) = high_nibble { emit hi << 4 }
  ```
- Hand-written; no external crate

## Critical considerations

- Whitespace is PDF spec section 7.2.2 (6 bytes); not Rust's char::is_whitespace
- Odd-length final pair: <3> decodes to 0x30 (NOT 0x03 — the dangling 3 is the HIGH nibble; low nibble is implicit 0)
- Non-hex non-whitespace non-> bytes emit STRUCT_INVALID_HEX diagnostic; decoder continues
- > terminator MUST be checked; bytes after > are ignored
- Empty stream <> decodes to empty bytes; not an error

## Acceptance criteria

- Round-trip: hex-encode 1 KB random bytes, decode → byte-identical
- Odd-length: <3> → [0x30], <ABC> → [0xAB, 0xC0]
- Mixed case: <aF> and <Af> both → [0xAF]
- Whitespace ignored: <A B C D> → [0xAB, 0xCD]
- Bytes outside [0-9A-Fa-f\\s>] emit STRUCT_INVALID_HEX; decoder continues

## References

- Plan section: Phase 1.5 Stream Decoder
- PDF spec 7.4.2 ASCIIHexDecode
- Phase 1.1 STRUCT_INVALID_HEX diagnostic convention
- Coordinator: pdftract-17rcj (parent — three ASCII filters bundle)
Labels: asciihex, decoder, phase-1
issue.title: Implement ASCIIHexDecode filter (odd-length zero padding + > terminator)

issue.description:
## Scope

Implement the 8 overlay-layer renderers that build the SVG groups for the inspector. Each layer is independently toggleable via CSS classes (toggled by 7.9.3 frontend). Layers: spans (outline rects color-coded by confidence), blocks (translucent rects by kind), columns (dashed vertical column-boundary lines), reading-order (curved numbered arrows), confidence-heatmap (per-glyph color cells), OCR-regions (cyan diagonal stripes on Tesseract regions), MCID (numeric labels in marked-content corners), anchors (block-id labels at top-left).

## Why this matters

These overlays are the inspector's value. Each one answers a specific debugging question:
- spans: is each visible word a single span or fragmented?
- blocks: is the page grouped into the right blocks?
- columns: did pdftract detect the column structure correctly?
- reading-order: in what order did pdftract decide to read?
- confidence-heatmap: which glyphs is pdftract unsure about?
- OCR: which regions came from Tesseract instead of vector text?
- MCID: which marked-content tags govern which regions?
- anchors: what Markdown anchor IDs will downstream output produce?

## Implementation guidance

- Per-layer helpers, each returning a Vec<svg::Node>:
  - render_spans(spans: &[Span]) -> Vec<SvgNode>: outline rect per span; stroke color = confidence_to_color(c) (red < 0.5, yellow 0.5-0.8, green > 0.8)
  - render_blocks(blocks: &[Block]) -> Vec<SvgNode>: translucent fill rect per block; fill color = kind_to_color(k) (heading blue, paragraph gray, table teal, list purple, code orange, header_footer light gray, figure brown, caption pink)
  - render_columns(cols: &[ColumnBoundary]) -> Vec<SvgNode>: dashed vertical line at each column boundary; "Col N" label at page top
  - render_reading_order(blocks: &[Block], order: &[usize]) -> Vec<SvgNode>: SVG <path d="M{x1},{y1} Q{cx},{cy} {x2},{y2}"/> from block center to next block center; numeric labels 1, 2, 3, ... on each block
  - render_confidence_heatmap(spans: &[Span]) -> Vec<SvgNode>: small filled rect per glyph at the glyph position; color via confidence_to_color
  - render_ocr_regions(ocr: &[OcrRegion]) -> Vec<SvgNode>: cyan diagonal stripe pattern (SVG <pattern>) filled into each OCR region
  - render_mcid_labels(mcid_map: &HashMap<u32, BlockRef>) -> Vec<SvgNode>: small <text> with MCID number in top-right corner of each block bbox
  - render_anchor_labels(blocks: &[Block]) -> Vec<SvgNode>: small <text> with block.id (e.g. "block_42") at top-left of each block bbox
- All layers wrapped in <g class="layer-<name>">; CSS in 7.9.3 toggles visibility
- Color encodings centralised in inspector::colors module
- Tooltip data: each span outline rect has data-* attrs (data-text, data-font, data-confidence, data-bbox, data-block, data-mcid, data-reading-idx); frontend (7.9.3) reads on hover to populate tooltip
- Reading-order arrows: bezier control point at (midx, midy + 10pt) for visible curve; numeric label at midpoint
- Confidence-heatmap is the densest layer (one rect per glyph) - generate carefully to keep SVG payload manageable

## Critical considerations

- CSS-only toggling means all 8 layer groups present in EVERY page SVG, even when toggled off; payload size considered when designing layers
- Confidence-heatmap can balloon SVG; consider sampling (only show 1 in 4 glyphs) for very glyph-dense pages
- OCR layer only present when page is Scanned or Hybrid; absent on pure Vector pages
- MCID layer only present when page has marked content (Phase 3.4)
- Reading-order arrows: limit to the FIRST N (e.g. 50) blocks; otherwise arrows clutter; mention truncation in toolbar
- Color encoding consistent with plan section 2837-2845 - don't invent new colors

## Acceptance criteria

- 8 layer functions implemented, each returning Vec<SvgNode>
- All 8 layer groups present in SVG output with correct class names
- Color encodings match plan
- data-* attrs on span rects feed tooltip
- Critical test (from plan): all eight layer toggles produce DOM changes (verified via headless-browser test in 7.9.3)
- Public layers::render_all(page: &ExtractedPage) -> Vec<LayerGroup>

## References

- Plan section: 7.9 lines 2836-2845 (layer table)
- 7.9.4 (SVG renderer scaffold)
- 7.9.3 (CSS toggle consumer)
- 7.9.6 (hover tooltip consumer of data-* attrs)

issue.description:
## Scope

Coordinator for sub-phase 3.5: detect and skip BI/ID/EI inline image sequences in a content stream without confusing the parser about subsequent text operators. Per spec sec 8.9.7, BI introduces a key-value image header, ID switches to raw image bytes, EI terminates the image; the EI delimiter must be preceded by whitespace.

## Why this matters

Inline images are uncommon but legal; if the content stream parser does not recognize them, every byte of image data is misinterpreted as PDF operator tokens producing parse errors or worse — running random binary bytes as operators. Correctly skipping inline images is a robustness requirement for parsing real-world PDFs.

## Children

- BI/ID inline image header parser
- ID-to-EI raw-bytes scanner (whitespace-preceded EI detection)
- ImageXObject record creation (page image list grows by 1 entry per inline image)

## Critical considerations

- The ID..EI delimiter is the ONLY raw-bytes range in a content stream; everything else is token-structured.
- EI must be preceded by whitespace (space, tab, CR, LF, FF) per spec — naive "find first EI" fails on image data containing the byte sequence "EI".
- Inline images contribute to the page's image list (Phase 4.4 needs them for figure-block detection).

## Acceptance criteria

- All 3 children closed.
- Inline image immediately followed by text operators: text operators parsed correctly after EI.
- Inline image data containing the byte sequence "EI" in the middle: not treated as terminator (must be preceded by whitespace).

## References

- Plan section: Phase 3.5 Inline Images (lines 1592-1600)
- ISO 32000-1 sec 8.9.7

SHA-256 hash of decoded font program bytes looked up in compile-time phf::Map<[u8; 32], [(u16, u32)]>. build.rs: generate_font_fingerprints() reads JSON and generates static map. src/font/fingerprint.rs: FontFingerprint, CachedFingerprint, lookup API. Empty JSON compiles to valid empty phf::Map. 12 tests PASS. Commit 3082cdb. See notes/pdftract-njde.md
issue.description:
## Scope

Implement Level 3 of the encoding fallback chain. Hash the raw decoded font program bytes (`/FontFile`, `/FontFile2`, or `/FontFile3`) with SHA-256 and look up the 32-byte digest in a compile-time `phf::Map<[u8; 32], &'static [(u16, char)]>`. The value slice maps glyph ids to Unicode codepoints for that exact font binary. Initially populated with the top ~200 commercial fonts.

## Why this matters

Many publishers embed the same proprietary font (Frutiger, Akzidenz-Grotesk, custom corporate fonts) across millions of PDFs. When `/ToUnicode` is missing AND the embedded font subset has stripped glyph names, only a content-based hash can recover Unicode. This level closes the gap between Level 2 (named encoding) and Level 4 (visual shape recognition) for known fonts.

## Implementation guidance

- Crate: `sha2` (Sha256 trait). Already approved in Dependency Matrix.
- Source artifact: `crates/pdftract-core/build/font-fingerprints.json` — list of `{ sha256_hex, font_name (informational), entries: [[gid, codepoint], ...] }`.
- `build.rs`: read JSON, validate sha256 hex (32 bytes), validate codepoints are valid Unicode scalars, then `phf_codegen::Map::build()` keyed by `[u8; 32]`.
- Runtime API: `pub fn lookup_font_fingerprint(font_program_bytes: &[u8], gid: u16) -> Option<char>`.
- Compute hash ONCE per Font load, store on the Font struct; do not re-hash per glyph.
- Skip L3 if no embedded font program (Std-14 fonts) — defensive guard per plan.

## Critical considerations

- INV: phf::Map key MUST be `[u8; 32]`, not `&str`. The hex string in JSON is a development convenience; conversion to bytes happens at build time.
- Binary footprint target: ~500 KB for 200 fonts averaging 1000 glyphs each. Verify via `cargo bloat`.
- The font-fingerprints.json is the authoritative artifact; PRs add entries here, build.rs regenerates the static.
- Database is not user-extensible at runtime — this is by design; runtime extension would require either lockfile management or unsound dynamic linking.
- ADR: Hash is over the DECODED stream bytes (post FlateDecode etc.), pre-interpretation. Same font with different filter encodings must produce the same hash.

## Acceptance criteria

- Empty JSON produces a valid (empty) phf::Map; no compile failure.
- Test fixture font_program -> SHA-256 -> phf::Map lookup -> expected (gid, char) entries.
- Lookup of unknown digest returns None.
- Hash is stable across runs.
- Binary footprint < 500 KB for the bundled DB.

## References

- Plan section: Phase 2.2 Level 3 (lines 1343-1352)
- "Database spec" paragraph (line 1347)
issue.title: Font fingerprint cache (Level 3) and build-time DB pipeline

issue.close_reason: Implemented char-weighted median readability aggregation per acceptance criteria. All tests pass. Verification note at notes/pdftract-oh30a.md. Commit 9970935.
issue.description:
## Scope

Implement `aggregate_page_readability(spans: &[Span]) -> f32` that computes the per-page readability score as the MEDIAN of per-span readability scores WEIGHTED by character count (longer spans count more). Store the result in `page.extraction_quality.readability: f32`. The field is exposed in JSON output.

## Why this matters

Per-span scores are useful for diagnostics, but a per-page summary is what drives the BrokenVector escalation (sibling bead) and what end users see in extraction-quality metadata. Char-weighting prevents a few high-confidence short spans (e.g., header text "Page 1") from masking poor body extraction.

## Implementation guidance

- For each span: compute (score, char_count = span.text.chars().count()).
- Char-count-weighted median:
  - Sort spans by score ascending.
  - Cumulative char count.
  - Find the score at the half-total-char-count point.
- Implementation: collect `(score, count)` pairs; sort by score; sum counts; walk sorted list, accumulating count; return the score whose cumulative count first reaches `total_count / 2`.
- Edge case: total char count == 0 (empty page) -> return 0.0 or NaN (pick 0.0 for safety; no score is also acceptable but JSON serialization easier with f32).
- Single span: return its score.

## Critical considerations

- INV: median is weighted by char count; do NOT use simple median over spans (would over-weight short spans).
- Alternatives considered: mean (sensitive to outliers), 50th percentile (== median; same thing here). Plan picks "median weighted by span char count".
- Place output in `page.extraction_quality.readability`; the extraction_quality struct already exists from Phase 0/1 work (likely a struct PageExtractionQuality { readability: f32, /* other fields */ }).
- The score is exposed in JSON output (Phase 6.1); ensure serde rounds to 3 decimals or similar for clean output.

## Acceptance criteria

- Page with 1 span of 100 chars at score 0.9: page score = 0.9.
- Page with 3 spans: (100 chars, 0.9), (10 chars, 0.5), (100 chars, 0.8): char-weighted median walks sorted [0.5(10), 0.8(100), 0.9(100)], cumsum=[10, 110, 210]; half = 105; score at cumsum >= 105 is 0.8 -> page score = 0.8.
- Empty page: page score = 0.0 (default).
- All-perfect spans: page score = 1.0.

## References

- Plan section: Phase 4.7 Per-page readability score (line 1783)
issue.title: Per-page readability aggregation (median weighted by char count) + page.extraction_quality field

issue.description:
## Scope

Implement the `cm a b c d e f` operator: multiply the current transformation matrix (CTM) by the operand matrix `[[a,b,0],[c,d,0],[e,f,1]]`. This is the FUNDAMENTAL CTM mutation operator; all page-coordinate transforms compose through cm. Operates on graphics state (NOT text state — text matrices are independent and updated by Td/Tm).

## Why this matters

CTM is the device-to-user transform that ultimately maps every glyph's text-space bbox into page coordinates. Form XObjects, scaled drawings, rotations, mirror flips — all encoded as cm operators. A cm bug shifts/scales/rotates every glyph after it.

## Implementation guidance

- Pop 6 numbers from operand stack as f64. Validate count; emit `CM_ARG_COUNT` diagnostic on mismatch and discard.
- Construct: `M = [[a,b,0],[c,d,0],[e,f,1]]`.
- Update: `ctm = M * ctm`. (Order matters: spec says "premultiply", which means M is applied FIRST to user-space points before the existing CTM.)
- This operator is GENERALLY inside a q...Q pair (scope the transform) but legally allowed at top level (irrevocably modifies CTM for the rest of the page).
- The text_matrix and text_line_matrix are INDEPENDENT of CTM — text-space glyph bboxes are computed by `text_matrix * ctm` when emitted as glyphs (Phase 3.2).

## Critical considerations

- Order is `M * ctm`, not `ctm * M`. Test: `cm 2 0 0 2 0 0` (scale x2) followed by a glyph at text-space (1,1) should end up at device-space (2,2) — verify the math.
- f64 throughout: cumulative CTM in deep form XObjects can drift if f32 is used; the 8-byte cost is negligible compared to the f64 text matrices.
- Floating-point safety: extremely degenerate matrices (det == 0, NaN inputs) should be CLAMPED to identity with `CM_DEGENERATE` diagnostic to prevent infinite/NaN bboxes downstream.
- Form XObject /Matrix is applied via the SAME cm operation conceptually: before executing the XObject, push a fresh CTM frame, multiply in the form's matrix, then execute. Phase 3.3 handles this.

## Acceptance criteria

- `1 0 0 1 100 200 cm` (translate) shifts CTM origin by (100, 200).
- `2 0 0 2 0 0 cm` (scale) doubles ctm scale; a subsequent text glyph at text-space (1,1) maps to device-space (2,2).
- Order test: `cm 2 0 0 2 0 0` followed by `cm 1 0 0 1 10 0` (translate then scale check): determine which order spec mandates and verify with a regression test.
- Wrong arg count (5 or 7 numbers) emits diagnostic and discards.
- NaN input clamps to identity with diagnostic.

## References

- Plan section: Phase 3.1 CTM operators (line 1495)

issue.description:
## Scope

Implement the v1 fingerprint algorithm in `crates/pdftract-core/src/fingerprint/mod.rs`:

```rust
pub fn compute_fingerprint(doc: &Document) -> String {
    let mut hasher = Sha256::new();
    // 1. Page count (u32 BE)
    hasher.update(&(doc.pages.len() as u32).to_be_bytes());
    // 2. Per-page contributions
    for page in &doc.pages {
        // a. SHA-256 of concatenated decoded content streams
        // b. SHA-256 of resolved resource dict (canonical)
        // c. Page geometry, canonicalized
    }
    // 3. Structure tree hash (or zeros)
    // 4. Catalog feature flag byte
    format!("pdftract-v1:{}", hex::encode(hasher.finalize()))
}
```

## Implementation guidance

- Use sha2 = "0.10" crate (already in default deps)
- Use hex = "0.4" for hex encoding
- Content stream hash: decode each content stream via Phase 1.5, normalize whitespace to single 0x20 between tokens (re-tokenize via Phase 1.1 lexer), SHA-256 the normalized bytes
- Resource dict hash:
  - Iterate fonts in /Font dict keys SORTED LEXICALLY (deterministic order)
  - Each font: resolve ObjRef, compute "rendering-relevant" fingerprint (Phase 2 Level 3 contributes; for Phase 1 stub use SHA-256 of serialized PdfObject)
  - XObjects: serialize each XObject's stream bytes (decoded via Phase 1.5) + SHA-256
  - ExtGState: serialize each entry as canonical-JSON + SHA-256
  - Combine via Merkle hash
- Geometry canonicalization: each f64 -> i64 via `round_to_fixed_4dp(x) = (x * 10000.0).round_ties_even() as i64`; write 8-byte big-endian (32 bytes per BBox); Rotate as 4-byte BE i32
- Whitespace normalization: lex decoded stream, emit each token followed by single 0x20, drop original whitespace
- Structure tree hash: recursive walk over /StructTreeRoot, serialize each /S, /Lang, /Alt, /ActualText, canonical-JSON + SHA-256

## Critical considerations

- Critical test: same PDF re-saved by Acrobat and pdftk -> SAME fingerprint (xref/metadata differ; content does not)
- Critical test: /CreationDate-only-changed -> SAME fingerprint (metadata excluded per ADR-008)
- Critical test: one glyph removed in 100-page PDF -> DIFFERENT fingerprint
- Critical test: 10 invocations on same file -> identical (INV-3)
- KU-7: linearized PDF vs qpdf --linearize-off -> SAME fingerprint
- `round_ties_even` (banker's rounding) is REQUIRED — not IEEE-754 default
- For Phase 1, font-fingerprint dependency (Phase 2 Level 3) is not yet implemented; use STUB that hashes raw font dict bytes. Document that this stub exists and will be replaced in Phase 2
- Algorithm must be SINGLE-THREADED-DETERMINISTIC; do NOT use rayon
- Performance: 100-page PDF fingerprint in < 100 ms (mostly SHA-256 throughput)
- "pdftract-v1:" prefix is INV-13; do not omit even for internal use cases

## Acceptance criteria

- compute_fingerprint() returns "pdftract-v1:" + 64-hex for any valid Document
- INV-3: 100 calls on same Document produce identical string
- INV-13: regex `^pdftract-v1:[0-9a-f]{64}$` matches every output
- KU-7: linearized fixture's fingerprint == qpdf-delinearized fixture's
- Performance: 100-page PDF in < 100 ms
- INV-8 maintained

## References

- Plan section: Phase 1.7 lines 1186-1219 (algorithm inputs + exclusions + acceptance)
- ADR-008 (exclusion rationale)
- INV-3, INV-13, KU-7
- Dependency Matrix: sha2 (default)

issue.description:
## Scope

Implement the top-level resolver `resolve_unicode(font: &Font, char_code: &[u8]) -> ResolvedGlyph` that drives all four levels of the encoding fallback chain in order and produces a `(SmallVec<[char; 4]>, UnicodeSource, f32)` result. Owns the per-font `(char_code -> resolution)` LRU cache and emits the `GLYPH_UNMAPPED` diagnostic exactly once per (font, code) miss.

## Why this matters

The resolver is the public API for Phase 2 consumed by Phase 3 content stream execution. It must be cheap on cache hit (no allocations, no logging), correct on cache miss (returns the highest-confidence source), and observable on failure (a single diagnostic per missed code, not one per occurrence — TJ arrays can hit the same code thousands of times).

## Implementation guidance

- State machine: try L1 (ToUnicode) -> if non-empty non-U+FFFD return; else L2 (named encoding + Differences + AGL) -> if Some return; else L3 (font fingerprint cache) -> if Some return; else L4 (call into pdftract-core::font::shape::recognize from Phase 2.5) -> if Some return; else U+FFFD with `unknown` source.
- Cache: a `DashMap<(FontId, SmallVec<[u8; 4]>), ResolvedGlyph>` on the Font (or its parent FontCache). FontId is the Arc::as_ptr cast to usize.
- Diagnostics: maintain a `HashSet<(FontId, SmallVec<[u8; 4]>)>` of already-emitted misses; first miss emits diagnostic, subsequent misses for same key are silent.
- L1 short-circuit: a Some result of `[U+FFFD]` or `[]` MUST fall through. Anything else commits.
- Multi-codepoint results from L1 (ligature expansion) carry the SAME confidence 1.0 — each char in the returned slice is treated as a separate output glyph with cloned source/confidence by the content stream layer.

## Critical considerations

- Cache eviction: LRU not required for v0.1.0 — fonts in a single PDF have bounded code space (< 65536 codes per font * < 100 fonts < ~6.5M entries worst case). Use unbounded map; document this.
- INV: ResolvedGlyph.confidence is always one of {1.0, 0.9, 0.85, 0.7, 0.0}.
- L4 may be `cfg`-gated behind `default-features = ["shape-db"]`. When disabled, the resolver skips L4 and emits diagnostic.
- Returning `[U+FFFD]` is the failure case; do NOT panic and do NOT skip the glyph entirely (downstream layout needs a glyph to position).
- Standard 14 fonts: skip L3 (no embedded program) per the plan's "defensive guard" note.

## Acceptance criteria

- A font with ToUnicode that maps code 0 to `fi` produces a 2-char slice with confidence 1.0.
- A font with no ToUnicode and WinAnsi encoding produces 1.0 for ASCII codes via L2 (wait, that's 0.9 — AGL path).
- An L1 miss with a successful L2 returns confidence 0.9 and source `agl`.
- An L1+L2 miss with a successful L3 returns confidence 0.85 and source `fingerprint`.
- An all-level miss returns `[U+FFFD]`, source `unknown`, confidence 0.0, AND emits the diagnostic exactly once even if called 1000 times for the same (font, code).
- INV: cache hit returns identical ResolvedGlyph as cache miss.

## References

- Plan section: Phase 2.2 entire (lines 1318-1370)
- INV: every glyph in output carries unicode_source field
issue.title: 4-level encoding resolver state machine + per-font miss cache

## Scope

Define Line { spans: Vec<Span>, bbox: [f32; 4] union, baseline: f32, direction: LineDirection, page_relative_y: f32 } and helper compute_baseline(span) -> f32 returning span.bbox[1] + (span.bbox[3] - span.bbox[1]) * 0.2. The 0.2 multiplier is plan's descender approximation.

## Why this matters

Line is 3rd-most-important struct (after Glyph, Span). Line bbox drives column detection and reading order; baseline drives clustering. Errors cascade.

## Implementation guidance

- Struct with LineDirection enum (Ltr, Rtl, Mixed).
- compute_baseline: trivial arithmetic per plan formula.
- ADR for 0.2 multiplier (empirical fit; refinement via font descender).
- bbox = UNION; baseline = average or median of member spans.
- page_relative_y = (page_height - bbox[3]) / page_height (0=top, 1=bottom) for reading order sorting.

## Critical considerations

- INV: baseline approximation consistent within page (all spans use same formula).
- 0.2 fits most Latin fonts; CJK/Arabic may differ.
- Zero-height span: baseline == y0 == y1, no error.
- Line.bbox tightness: exclude synthetic " " spans if Option (b) was used.

## Acceptance criteria

- Span bbox [0,100,50,110] (height 10): baseline = 102.
- Span bbox [0,100,50,100] (zero): baseline = 100.
- 3-span line: bbox is union.
- LineDirection serdes to "ltr"/"rtl"/"mixed".

issue.description:
## Scope

Implement the DPI selector that picks the rendering DPI per page from font-size signals (Phase 4 spans) plus image-filter signals (Phase 1.5). Returns a single u32 DPI used by both 5.2.1 direct-compositing and 5.2.2 pdfium paths.

## Why this matters

DPI is the single biggest correctness lever for OCR. 300 DPI is the sweet spot for 10pt body text; below that, character recognition WER spikes. Fine-print (legal documents, footnotes) needs 400 DPI to avoid character collisions. JBIG2 images are already binary at scan resolution; rendering at 300 DPI throws away no data but wastes ~9x the CPU. Setting DPI per page (not globally) is what keeps OCR fast on heterogeneous corpora.

## Implementation guidance

- Entry: fn select_dpi(page: &PageContext, image_filters: &[Pdf1Filter]) -> u32
- Algorithm:
  1. If any image filter is JBIG2Decode -> return 200
  2. If Phase 4 spans available, compute median font_size on the page
     - median < 7.0 pt -> 400 (fine print)
     - median >= 7.0 pt -> 300
  3. If no spans (truly scanned, no vector text), use 300 as default
- Make thresholds configurable via ExtractionOptions::ocr_dpi_override: Option<u32> for advanced users / debugging
- Document the lookup table in module rustdoc

## Critical considerations

- 200 DPI for JBIG2 is correct ONLY when the page contains a JBIG2 image; mixed page with JBIG2 + DCT should pick the higher DPI
- font_size signal from Phase 4 is the median (not mean) because outlier huge or tiny glyphs (drop caps, footers) would skew mean
- DPI is a u32; never store as f32 because pdfium-render takes integer DPI
- DPI choice MUST be recorded in extraction_quality so it appears in the JSON output footer (debuggability)

## Acceptance criteria

- Unit tests: each branch of the algorithm with synthetic inputs
- Integration: legal-document fixture (lots of 6pt footnotes) -> 400 DPI selected; standard textbook -> 300 DPI; pure JBIG2 fixture -> 200 DPI
- DPI override option works: ocr_dpi_override = Some(150) -> 150 used regardless of signals
- extraction_quality.dpi_used populated correctly

## References

- Plan section: Phase 5.2 DPI selection (lines 1858-1862)
- Phase 1.5 stream filters

issue.description:
## Scope

Build the property-testing harness and curated test corpus for the Lexer module:

1. **Property tests** under `tests/proptest/lexer.rs` (gated by `#[cfg(feature = "proptest")]`):
   - `prop_lexer_never_panics`: arbitrary byte vectors of size 0..16384 fed to Lexer; assert no panic; collect all tokens until Eof
   - `prop_string_roundtrip`: arbitrary printable byte strings wrapped in `(...)` with random escapes; assert Token::String decodes to original bytes (modulo line-ending normalization)
   - `prop_hex_roundtrip`: arbitrary byte vectors; hex-encode with random whitespace insertion; assert Token::String decodes to original
   - `prop_name_length_bound`: arbitrary byte sequences after `/`; assert resulting Token::Name's raw count <= 127
   - `prop_position_monotone`: arbitrary input; assert `Lexer::position()` is monotonically non-decreasing across calls to `next_token()`
   - `prop_invariant_inv8`: every input that reaches end-of-stream produces a `Vec<Diagnostic>` (possibly empty) and never panics

2. **Curated unit-test corpus** under `tests/lexer/fixtures/`:
   - `empty.bin` (0 bytes) — EC-01 test
   - `whitespace_only.bin` — `\t\n   \r\f\0   `
   - `every_token.pdf.in` — a hand-crafted snippet containing each token type once
   - `string_escapes.pdf.in` — every documented escape sequence and the critical-test inputs from each child bead
   - `name_edge_cases.pdf.in` — `#20`, `#00`, 127-byte name, 128-byte name (truncated), empty `/`, mixed hex casing
   - `hex_string_edge_cases.pdf.in` — odd length, embedded whitespace, mixed case, unterminated
   - `numeric_edge_cases.pdf.in` — `-.5`, `42.`, overflow, bare `+`, `1e5` (NOT scientific)
   - `bom_utf16_string.pdf.in` — string literal containing UTF-16BE BOM (FE FF) prefix; verify lexer returns raw bytes (decoding is Phase 1.4's job)

3. **Integration test runner** that walks `tests/lexer/fixtures/`, lexes each, and compares the token stream against a sibling `.tokens.txt` file (golden output). Update golden via `BLESS=1 cargo test`.

## Why this matters

The plan's Phase 0.5 mandate is 10,000+ proptest cases per parser module per PR. The lexer is the leaf module — its property tests are foundational to the whole parser stack. Curated fixtures cover the documented Critical tests from the plan; the proptest harness covers the long tail of "what if the bytes are weird".

## Implementation guidance

- proptest crate version: 1.x (already in Phase 0.5 plan)
- Use `proptest-derive` for `Arbitrary` impls on test-side helper types
- Strategies: `prop::collection::vec(any::<u8>(), 0..16384)` for arbitrary inputs; `r"\PC*"` (printable Unicode) for human-readable fragments
- Golden test approach: produce `.tokens.txt` via Debug formatting of each token, one per line; `bless` rewrites them
- proptest-regressions/ directory committed so minimal counterexamples persist across runs
- Cargo feature: `proptest = ["dep:proptest"]` so default builds skip the dependency

## Critical considerations

- proptest budget: ~10,000 cases per property; with 6 properties, total runtime ~1 CPU-min on a fast machine. Phase 0.5 budget is 1 CPU-hour for the whole parser, so the lexer's share is generous
- Some proptest assertions cannot be made strict: e.g. `prop_string_roundtrip` must allow for line-ending normalization (bare `\r` -> `\n`) per spec. Use `assert!` with explanatory messages so failures are interpretable
- Fixtures use `.pdf.in` extension (not `.pdf`) because they're snippets, not complete PDFs; this prevents test tools from trying to parse them as full PDFs
- The EC-01 empty-file test is critical: a 0-byte input must produce `Token::Eof` from the very first `next_token()` call without panicking. This is one of the most-cited Phase 1.1 critical tests
- Whitespace-only input is in EC-01's family: produces Eof without panic

## Acceptance criteria

- `cargo test --features proptest -p pdftract-core` exercises 6 lexer properties and passes
- `tests/lexer/fixtures/` contains the 8 listed fixture files with sibling `.tokens.txt` golden outputs
- A deliberate lexer panic (e.g. `unreachable!()` in name-lexer hot path) is caught by a property test
- proptest-regressions/ directory committed
- Empty file (EC-01) test passes: 0-byte input -> Token::Eof, no panic, no diagnostic
- Whitespace-only file test passes: only-whitespace input -> Token::Eof
- INV-8 verified by `prop_lexer_never_panics`

## References

- Plan section: Phase 1.1 line 1051 (whitespace-only file critical test)
- Phase 0.5 (proptest budget; nightly fuzz CronWorkflow)
- INV-8 (no panic in pdftract-core)
- EC-01 (Empty PDF)

issue.description:
## Scope

Implement the three marked-content operator parsers in the content-stream executor: BMC /Tag, BDC /Tag <<props>> or BDC /Tag /PropName, EMC. Each consumes its operands from the operand stack, dispatches to the marked-content stack (sibling bead) for push/pop, and emits diagnostics on misuse.

## Why this matters

Marked-content operators are the entry points; the marked-content stack (sibling) provides the data structure they manipulate. Splitting them allows the stack to be unit-tested independently of operator dispatch, and the operators to be unit-tested with a mock stack.

## Implementation guidance

- BMC: pops 1 operand (a Name). Calls stack.push_bmc(name).
- BDC: pops 2 operands (a Name and a dict/Name). Dispatches on the second operand's type:
  - If Name: resolve via ResourceStack::lookup_properties(name); on found-dict-with-MCID, read /MCID as u32; on not-found, emit UNKNOWN_MARKED_CONTENT_PROPS diagnostic and call stack.push_bdc(tag, None)
  - If Dict: read /MCID directly (if absent, None)
  - Otherwise: emit STRUCT_INVALID_BDC_OPERAND and call stack.push_bdc(tag, None)
- EMC: pops 0 operands. Calls stack.pop_emc(); on underflow, emit EMC_WITHOUT_BMC diagnostic
- Wire into the existing content-stream operator dispatch table

## Critical considerations

- BDC's second operand may be a Name (resource-table lookup) or a Dict (inline); the dispatch on PdfObject variant is the gotcha
- ResourceStack::lookup_properties returns the page resources' /Properties subdict entries; missing-property is NOT a panic
- /MCID values are u32 (\"non-negative integer\" per spec); widely seen values are 0-10000
- Operator dispatch must restore the operand stack to empty if these operators emit a diagnostic (don't leave half-consumed operands)
- INV: marked content stack is INDEPENDENT of graphics state stack — q/Q does NOT affect it (PDF spec 14.5)

## Acceptance criteria

- BMC /Span EMC parses without diagnostics
- BDC /Span <</MCID 42>> EMC parses; sibling stack records mcid=Some(42)
- BDC /P /MyProps EMC where /MyProps resolves to dict containing /MCID 7: mcid=Some(7)
- BDC /P /UnknownProps EMC: mcid=None + UNKNOWN_MARKED_CONTENT_PROPS diagnostic
- EMC without BMC: EMC_WITHOUT_BMC diagnostic; no panic; subsequent operators still work
- INV-8 (no panic) preserved on all malformed inputs
- Unit tests for each operator with mock ResourceStack

## References

- Plan section: Phase 3 marked-content operators
- PDF spec section 14.5 (Marked Content)
- Coordinator: pdftract-1l6wn (parent — operators + stack bundle)
- Sibling: marked-content stack data structure
Labels: operator, parser, phase-3

## Scope

Coordinator for sub-phase 3.1: build the full PDF graphics state machine consumed by every other Phase 3 child. Delivers the `GraphicsState` struct (13 fields including CTM, text matrices, font binding, all text-state parameters, fill/stroke color), the `Color` enum (DeviceGray, DeviceRGB, DeviceCMYK, Spot, Other), the q/Q stack with depth limit 64, all 14 text state operators (Tc/Tw/Tz/TL/Tf/Tr/Ts/Td/TD/Tm/T*/BT/ET), the CTM operator cm, the 6 color operators (rg, RG, k, K, cs, scn) reaching every text op, plus page /Rotate normalization applied to glyph bboxes after assembly.

## Why this matters

Without a correct graphics state machine, every layout downstream is wrong. Rotated pages produce sideways bboxes; nested q/Q without proper save/restore produces drifting transforms; Tm/Td ordering bugs corrupt every subsequent glyph position. Phase 3.2-3.5 all CONSUME the state machine — they cannot start before it works.

## Children

- GraphicsState struct + Color enum + CTM/text matrix initialization
- q/Q stack with depth limit 64 + GSTATE_STACK_OVERFLOW diagnostic
- Text state operators (Tc Tw Tz TL Ts Tr)
- Font binding (Tf) and text positioning operators (Td TD Tm T*)
- BT/ET text object lifecycle (resets text matrices to identity)
- Color operators (rg RG k K cs scn) populating fill_color/stroke_color
- CTM operator cm (matrix multiply)
- Page /Rotate normalization applied to all glyph bboxes after page assembly

## Critical considerations

- INV: q/Q stack depth limit is 64 per spec; level 65 emits diagnostic AND discards the push (safe failure, not abort).
- text_matrix is reset to identity on every BT; text_line_matrix tracks current line origin. ET DISCARDS both — operators after ET reuse no state.
- Td/TD/T* updates text_line_matrix first then COPIES it to text_matrix (per ISO 32000-1 9.4.4 Table 108).
- Color enum variants must include Spot(Arc<str>, f32) for spot colors and Other for unsupported (CalRGB/ICCBased/Pattern -> treated as transparent for text extraction).
- Page /Rotate 90/180/270: apply INVERSE rotation matrix to all glyph bboxes AFTER content stream execution so downstream operates in un-rotated space.

## Acceptance criteria

- All 8 children closed.
- q/Q 64 levels deep succeeds; 65th level emits GSTATE_STACK_OVERFLOW.
- Td chain accumulates correctly: `BT 100 200 Td 50 0 Td ET` yields text_matrix translation (150, 200).
- Tm followed by Td: Td is relative to previous text_line_matrix (not Tm).
- /Rotate 90: a glyph at (100, 100) with width 10 in original PDF coords becomes (page_height - 110, 100) post-normalization.
- All 6 color operators tracked: `0.5 0.5 0.5 rg` sets fill_color to DeviceRGB([0.5,0.5,0.5]).

## References

- Plan section: Phase 3.1 Graphics State Machine (lines 1440-1506)
- ISO 32000-1 Tables 51 (graphics state), 108 (text operators)
issue.title: Phase 3.1: Graphics State Machine (coordinator)

issue.description:
## Scope

Implement URL credential parsing for HTTPS URLs passed to pdftract: https://user:pass@host/path. The user:pass component is extracted, the URL is reconstructed without credentials (so it doesn't appear in logs), and credentials are passed to the HttpRangeSource as HTTP Basic auth.

Module: crates/pdftract-cli/src/cli.rs (or shared with HttpRangeSource construction) + url = \"2\" crate.

## Why this matters

URL-embedded credentials are the standard short-form for one-off authenticated HTTPS fetches (S3 presigned URLs, internal artifact stores with HTTP Basic). Without parsing them, pdftract would either reject these URLs (incompatible) or pass them through unchanged (leaking creds in logs, ureq error messages, and in HTTP request lines on the wire to TLS-MITM-aware proxies).

## Implementation guidance

- Crate: url = \"2\" (already a transitive dep typically; add if not)
- Parser:
  ```rust
  use url::Url;
  pub fn extract_url_credentials(url_str: &str) -> Result<(String, Option<(String, String)>)> {
      let url = Url::parse(url_str)?;
      let creds = if !url.username().is_empty() {
          Some((url.username().to_string(), url.password().unwrap_or(\"\").to_string()))
      } else { None };
      // Reconstruct URL without credentials
      let mut clean = url.clone();
      let _ = clean.set_username(\"\");
      let _ = clean.set_password(None);
      Ok((clean.to_string(), creds))
  }
  ```
- On HttpRangeSource construction, if creds are Some, add an Authorization: Basic <base64(user:pass)> header
- Cleaned URL is the one used in logs, error messages, and the Host header on the wire
- URL-decoding: url::Url::username() and password() return percent-decoded strings (correct for HTTP Basic encoding which then re-encodes via base64)

## Critical considerations

- Logs MUST use the cleaned URL; never the credential-embedded form. Audit log/tracing call sites to confirm
- HTTP Basic over plain HTTP (not HTTPS) is forbidden by best practice; reject http:// URLs with embedded creds at CLI parse with a clear error
- Empty username → no credentials extracted (None returned)
- Empty password → still treated as credentials (some APIs accept username-only with empty pwd); pass empty pwd
- URL credentials lose priority to --header Authorization: ... (user-explicit overrides URL-embedded); document and test
- The base64 encoding of \"user:pass\" must NOT URL-encode the colon (RFC 7617); use the standard base64 of the bytes
- Credentials in URL are case-sensitive (per RFC 3986); preserve case

## Acceptance criteria

- extract_url_credentials(\"https://alice:secret@example.com/doc.pdf\") → (\"https://example.com/doc.pdf\", Some((\"alice\", \"secret\")))
- extract_url_credentials(\"https://example.com/doc.pdf\") → (\"https://example.com/doc.pdf\", None)
- extract_url_credentials(\"http://alice:secret@example.com/doc.pdf\") → Err (http with creds rejected)
- Cleaned URL appears in logs; original URL with creds NEVER appears
- HttpRangeSource constructed with creds adds correct Authorization: Basic header (base64-decode and compare in test)
- --header Authorization: Bearer xyz overrides URL-embedded creds (user-explicit wins)
- URL-encoded credentials (https://alice%40example.com:secret@host/) decode correctly to alice@example.com

## References

- Plan section: Phase 1.8 + remote CLI cross-cut
- url crate: https://crates.io/crates/url
- RFC 3986 (URI syntax)
- RFC 7617 (HTTP Basic)
- Coordinator: pdftract-25igv (parent)
Labels: auth, phase-1, remote, url
issue.title: URL credential parsing (https://user:pass@host/path) — extract via url crate; reconstruct URL without creds

issue.description:
## Scope

Parse the `/ToUnicode` stream of a PDF font as a PostScript CMap program and produce a `ToUnicodeMap` that maps source byte sequences to Unicode codepoint slices. Implements the CMap subset required by ToUnicode: `beginbfchar`/`endbfchar`, `beginbfrange`/`endbfrange` (both contiguous and explicit-array forms), `usecmap`, comment stripping (`%`).

## Why this matters

Level 1 is the only level that gives confidence 1.0. Real-world coverage of well-formed PDFs hits L1 for ~70% of glyphs. Bugs here cascade into incorrect Unicode for every well-formed glyph in the document.

## Implementation guidance

- Treat the ToUnicode stream as PostScript tokens (numbers, hex strings `<...>`, names `/foo`, arrays `[...]`, keywords). Tokenizer is shared with content stream parsing — reuse if available, otherwise write a focused one here.
- `beginbfchar` ... `endbfchar` block: pairs of `<srcHex> <dstHex>`. Source is 1-4 bytes (decode hex). Destination is UTF-16BE; may decode to multiple chars (e.g. ligature expansion). Store as `(SmallVec<[u8; 4]>, SmallVec<[char; 4]>)`.
- `beginbfrange` ... `endbfrange` block: triples. Two forms:
  - `<lo> <hi> <dst>` — contiguous: code lo -> dst, lo+1 -> dst+1, ...
  - `<lo> <hi> [<d0> <d1> ...]` — explicit array; length must equal hi-lo+1.
- `usecmap`: parse the name token preceding `usecmap` and load the named CMap from the predefined CMap registry (Phase 2.3 ships these — for now stub returns empty map and emits diagnostic if unknown).
- Comment stripping: any `%` outside a string starts a comment until newline.

## Critical considerations

- Multi-codepoint destinations are MANDATORY (the `fi` ligature test is a primary acceptance criterion).
- Contiguous bfrange where dst is multi-codepoint is technically illegal per spec but seen in the wild — accept it, increment only the last codepoint.
- Source codes may have varying byte widths within the SAME CMap (1-byte for ASCII, 2-byte for CJK ranges); store as variable-length keys.
- Lookups are HOT; build a `HashMap<SmallVec<[u8; 4]>, SmallVec<[char; 4]>>` or split into per-byte-width maps for speed.
- Empty destination `<>` -> map to empty slice; caller falls through to L2.

## Acceptance criteria

- `beginbfchar <00> <FB01> endbfchar` parses (note: U+FB01 is the `fi` ligature) and the entry expands correctly when the dst is given as `<00660069>` (multi-codepoint).
- `beginbfrange <0041> <005A> <0041> endbfrange` maps A..=Z to U+0041..=U+005A.
- `beginbfrange <0001> <0003> [<FB01> <FB02> <FB03>] endbfrange` maps codes 1,2,3 to ligatures fi, fl, ffi.
- Comment lines `% foo` ignored.
- WinAnsi 0x92 -> U+2019 test passes when ToUnicode says so.

## References

- Plan section: Phase 2.2 Level 1 (lines 1322-1331)
- Critical tests: multi-codepoint bfchar, beginbfrange explicit array (line 1364-1365)
issue.title: ToUnicode CMap parser (Level 1)

issue.description:
## Scope

Create the crates/pdftract-libpdftract crate as the fourth workspace member of the pdftract repo. Configure Cargo.toml with crate-type = [\"cdylib\", \"staticlib\"] (both shared and static for downstream flexibility). The crate links pdftract-core as a regular Rust dependency; only the public extern \"C\" surface is exposed.

## Why this matters

The libpdftract C/C++ SDK requires its own crate to control the FFI surface (extern \"C\" functions, no Rust traits/generics in the export surface), the cdylib output type (.so / .dylib / .dll), and the staticlib output type (libpdftract.a for static linking). Mixing this surface into pdftract-core or pdftract-cli would force a different crate-type and bloat their build matrix.

## Implementation guidance

- Create crates/pdftract-libpdftract/Cargo.toml:
  ```toml
  [package]
  name = \"pdftract-libpdftract\"
  version.workspace = true
  license.workspace = true
  edition = \"2021\"

  [lib]
  crate-type = [\"cdylib\", \"staticlib\"]

  [dependencies]
  pdftract-core = { path = \"../pdftract-core\" }
  serde_json = \"1\"
  libc = \"0.2\"

  [build-dependencies]
  cbindgen = \"0.27\"
  ```
- Update root Cargo.toml workspace.members to include \"crates/pdftract-libpdftract\"
- Create crates/pdftract-libpdftract/src/lib.rs with module declarations (api, header_gen, etc.)
- Configure cdylib output naming convention via Cargo.toml (libpdftract.so on Linux, libpdftract.dylib on macOS, pdftract.dll on Windows)

## Critical considerations

- Crate name pdftract-libpdftract is intentional (sibling crate naming with double prefix); the .so/.dylib/.dll filename is libpdftract (no -lib- prefix) — controlled by setting [lib] name = \"pdftract\" if needed, but default Cargo behavior strips the leading lib- on Unix automatically
- Both cdylib AND staticlib crate-types in one [lib] is supported by Cargo and produces both artifacts in one build
- pdftract-core is a pure-Rust workspace dependency; the libpdftract crate only translates between extern \"C\" types and Rust types
- The version/license/edition fields use [workspace.package] inheritance to stay in sync with sibling crates

## Acceptance criteria

- cargo build -p pdftract-libpdftract produces target/debug/libpdftract.so (Linux), libpdftract.dylib (macOS), pdftract.dll (Windows), and libpdftract.a / pdftract.lib (static)
- Workspace cargo build builds all 4 crates without breaking existing crates
- cargo metadata shows pdftract-libpdftract in the workspace members
- Symbol table on libpdftract.so via nm -D shows no exported symbols yet (the API is empty in this bead; sibling bead populates)

## References

- Plan section: Phase SDK epic (C/C++ SDK row in the SDK Methods Surface table)
- Cargo docs: cdylib + staticlib crate-types
- Coordinator: pdftract-1eaxm (parent)
Labels: cpp, phase-6, scaffold, sdk

issue.description:
## Scope

Implement --md-anchors positional HTML-comment markers. Each block emits a single-line comment immediately before its content: <!-- pdftract: page=N block=N bbox=[x,y,w,h] kind=K -->. The comment format is a stable schema parseable by one regex; HTML comments are passthrough in every major Markdown renderer.

## Why this matters

Anchors let downstream tools (LLM agents, audit tools, document Q&A systems) map a Markdown excerpt back to a precise PDF location. The plan emphasizes (line 2197) that HTML comments are passthrough in GitHub, GitLab, Obsidian, Notion import, pulldown-cmark, marked, markdown-it — so anchored output stays human-readable while machines can recover positional metadata.

## Implementation guidance

- Flag: --md-anchors (CLI), ExtractionOptions.markdown_anchors: bool
- Per block, before emission:
  format!("<!-- pdftract: page={} block={} bbox=[{:.1},{:.1},{:.1},{:.1}] kind={} -->\n",
          page_idx, block_idx, x0, y0, x1, y1, kind_str)
- Parser regex (also implemented + tested):
  r"<!-- pdftract: page=(\d+) block=(\d+) bbox=\[([\d.,]+)\] kind=(\w+) -->"
- Block index is per-page (0-based within page), NOT global
- bbox precision: 1 decimal place (matches Phase 5.4.4 internal precision)
- kind matches the JSON page_type schema enum values (text-not-relevant — block kind not page kind; e.g. "heading", "paragraph")
- Provide a small parser library: pdftract::markdown::parse_anchors(md: &str) -> Vec<Anchor>

## Critical considerations

- Comment is ONE LINE (no embedded newline); CommonMark allows multi-line comments but single-line keeps regex simple
- HTML comments INSIDE a code fence are not recognized (renderers emit them verbatim); document this edge case
- Round-trip property: parse anchored MD -> recover the original block list (modulo inline styling, which is lossy)
- Reproducibility: same input -> identical anchor format
- The regex is a STABLE PUBLIC API; documented in docs/integrations/markdown-anchors.md (add to allowlist if needed)

## Acceptance criteria

- --md-anchors flag emits comment before every block
- Parser regex extracts page, block, bbox, kind from sample output
- Round-trip test: extract -> parse anchors -> matches original block list
- Comment doesn't interfere with CommonMark rendering (verified via pulldown-cmark roundtrip)
- bbox precision: 1 decimal place exact

## References

- Plan section: Phase 6.5 positional anchors (lines 2183-2197)

## Why this matters

The receipt profile ships in v1.0.0 as one of the nine built-ins (line 3040). Receipts are a high-volume document type for expense tracking and accounting tools; getting merchant, date, total, and payment_method right is the user-visible success metric.

## Implementation guidance

- File: profiles/builtin/receipt.yaml

  - description: "Sales receipts, store slips, restaurant checks"
  - priority: 10 (lower than invoice to avoid competing on invoice-shaped receipts)
  - match: all: [any: [text_contains: ['Receipt', 'Subtotal', 'Cash', 'Change Due', 'Thank you for your business'], heading_matches: '^Receipt\b'], structural.page_count: {min: 1, max: 2}]; none: [text_contains: ['Invoice #', 'Bill To']]

- Receipts are heavily monospaced -- table_detection: borderless_only is critical (strict_borders rejects everything)

issue.description:
## Scope

Implement classify_caption(block, page_context) that returns true if the block has small font (median font size < page body median) AND follows a Figure block within 2 line heights AND in the same column. Sets block.kind = Caption.

Module: crates/pdftract-core/src/layout/caption.rs.

## Why this matters

Figure+caption pairs are the most-common annotation pattern in scholarly papers, technical docs, and reports. Tagging captions enables: extracting figure-caption pairs as structured data, generating alt-text alternatives, and improving Markdown output (italic caption convention).

## Implementation guidance

- Caption detection criteria (all required):
  1. block.median_font_size < page_body_median (smaller than body text)
  2. vertical_distance(block.top, prev_figure.bottom) < 2 * line_height
  3. block is in same column as prev_figure (column membership from Phase 4.4)
- Apply after Figure detection (sibling); operates on the post-figure-insertion block list
- Iterate blocks in page order:
  - For each block, check if previous block is a Figure
  - If yes, evaluate the 3 criteria
  - If all pass, set block.kind = Caption
- page_body_median is the median font size across all paragraph blocks (computed once per page)
- line_height is the typical line spacing on the page (Phase 4.2 has this)

## Critical considerations

- The 2-line gap threshold is calibrated: captions are typically immediately below figures (within 1-2 lines); larger gaps suggest unrelated content
- Same-column check uses Phase 4.4 column boundaries; if the page has no columns (single-column), every block is in the same column
- Multi-line captions: only the first line's block is classified as Caption; subsequent caption lines are typically merged into the same block by Phase 4 line-grouping
- This is a soft classification; the block remains a paragraph if criteria don't all pass

## Acceptance criteria

- Block immediately below a Figure, with small font, same column → kind: Caption
- Block 5 lines below a Figure → no caption classification (gap too large)
- Block with body-size font below a Figure → no caption (font not smaller)
- Block in different column from Figure → no caption
- Markdown emission of Caption block: emit as italic (Phase 6.5 convention)

## References

- Plan section: Phase 4 caption detection
- Phase 4.2 line height
- Phase 4.4 column boundaries
- Coordinator: pdftract-25k4x (parent)
- Sibling: figure detection
Labels: caption, classifier, phase-4
issue.title: Caption block classifier (small font + follows Figure within 2 lines, same column)

## Scope

Build the maturin wheel-build pipeline for 5 target triples (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, x86_64-apple-darwin, aarch64-apple-darwin, x86_64-pc-windows-gnu). Author Argo WorkflowTemplate pdftract-py-ci in jedarden/declarative-config -> k8s/iad-ci/argo-workflows/. Wheels upload to PyPI on milestone tags.

## Why this matters

A binary Python wheel is the only viable distribution method for a Rust extension. Source distribution requires users to have a Rust toolchain (untenable for data scientists). Cross-compilation from a single Linux runner is the only sane way to produce all 5 wheels in one CI run.

## Implementation guidance

- Build tool: maturin (PEP 517 compliant)
- Linux x86_64 / aarch64: ghcr.io/rust-cross/manylinux base images
- macOS x86_64 / aarch64: osxcross toolchain via cross
- Windows x86_64: cross with x86_64-pc-windows-gnu target
- Argo WorkflowTemplate pdftract-py-ci:
  - Stage 1: build wheels for all 5 triples in parallel (5 steps)
  - Stage 2: collect artifacts from each step
  - Stage 3 (tag only): twine upload to PyPI using PYPI_TOKEN from sealed-secret
- WorkflowTemplate lives in jedarden/declarative-config -> k8s/iad-ci/argo-workflows/pdftract-py-ci.yaml
- ArgoCD syncs the WorkflowTemplate; submit manually for testing or via webhook on tag push
- Wheel filenames follow pep-491 (e.g. pdftract-1.0.0-cp310-cp310-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl)

## Critical considerations

- aarch64 macOS targets require explicit toolchain; document the cross setup
- manylinux glibc baseline: pick manylinux_2_28 (matches Ubuntu 22.04) for max compat
- Windows GNU vs MSVC: use GNU (cross-friendly); document the choice
- PyPI upload uses API token stored in sealed-secret pypi-token in argo-workflows namespace
- Test stage runs cibuildwheel-style smoke test (import pdftract; pdftract.extract on a tiny fixture) per wheel
- Argo WorkflowTemplate name MUST match pattern in cluster's WorkflowTemplates list

- Wheel install + smoke test passes on each triple

issue.description:
## Scope

Author tests/security/TH-05-ssrf-block.rs that exercises a comprehensive set of SSRF payloads against the remote-source fetcher (Phase 1.8) and the MCP extract tool (when given a URL). Asserts that schemes other than https:// are refused, that localhost, RFC1918 private ranges, IPv6 ULAs, link-local addresses, and cloud-metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254, fd00:ec2::254, etc.) are refused with a URL_PRIVATE_NETWORK diagnostic unless --allow-private-networks is set.

## Why this matters

TH-05 (line 876) addresses the SSRF attack class. The most common real-world SSRF target is the cloud metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254 which returns AWS IAM credentials; without this protection, any pdftract instance running on AWS that accepts a user-supplied URL could leak the host instance's credentials. The test fixture covers the full address space of dangerous targets to prevent regressions where a new private range is missed.

## Implementation guidance

- Test file: tests/security/TH-05-ssrf-block.rs
- Payload categories (each MUST be refused by default):
  - Cloud metadata: 169.254.169.254 (AWS), 100.100.100.200 (Alibaba), 168.63.129.16 (Azure), metadata.google.internal (GCP)
  - RFC1918 IPv4: 10.0.0.1, 172.16.0.1, 192.168.1.1, plus the boundaries (10.255.255.255, 172.31.255.255, 192.168.255.255)
  - Loopback: 127.0.0.1, 127.0.0.2, 127.255.255.255
  - Link-local IPv4: 169.254.0.1
  - IPv6 ULA: fd00::1, fc00::1
  - IPv6 loopback: ::1
  - IPv6 link-local: fe80::1
  - DNS that resolves to a private address: a hostname (test.localhost?) that resolves to 127.0.0.1
  - Schemes other than https: http://example.com, ftp://example.com, file:///etc/passwd, gopher://example.com
- For each payload:
  - Attempt extraction via pdftract extract --url <payload>: assert exit 64 OR 65 (depending on whether refusal is usage or data error -- pick one and document) with URL_PRIVATE_NETWORK diagnostic on stderr
  - Attempt the MCP extract tool with the same URL via a stdio harness: assert MCP error response with the diagnostic
  - In --serve mode: assert HTTP 400 with the diagnostic in the response body
- Positive test: with --allow-private-networks set, the same URLs are accepted (the test does NOT actually fetch, just asserts the refusal does not trigger)

## Critical considerations

- DNS resolution MUST happen ONCE in pdftract, NOT separately at fetch time -- otherwise DNS-rebinding attacks bypass the check
- The check operates on the RESOLVED IP, not the hostname; resolve, then check
- IPv6 zone IDs (fe80::1%eth0) need explicit handling -- treat the zone-id form as link-local regardless of zone
- URL parsing edge cases: HTTP basic auth credentials (https://user:pass@host/) -- the host is what matters; %-encoded host chars must be decoded before address parsing
- Scheme refusal is separate from address refusal; both refusals share the URL_PRIVATE_NETWORK diagnostic (or a sibling URL_SCHEME_REFUSED if implemented separately) -- the test asserts one of the two depending on implementation
- The --allow-private-networks flag MUST be loud: emit a WARN log line on startup if set ("WARNING: --allow-private-networks set; private/loopback addresses will be fetched. Do not enable in multi-tenant deployments.")
- The fetcher is in Phase 1.8 (ureq-based); same code path serves the MCP and serve surfaces

## Acceptance criteria

- tests/security/TH-05-ssrf-block.rs exists and passes
- All listed payloads (15+ across categories) trigger refusal in CLI / MCP / serve modes
- URL_PRIVATE_NETWORK diagnostic emitted
- --allow-private-networks bypass works
- Startup warning emitted when --allow-private-networks is set
- DNS resolution happens once and the resolved address is what is checked

## References

- Plan: line 876 (TH-05 entry), Phase 1.8 (remote HTTP fetcher), ureq feature flag, Diagnostic Code Catalog URL_PRIVATE_NETWORK
